title: Electric field control of anisotropic spin traffic between spin-filtering and magnon-scattering in a layered antiferromagnet
authors: Mohamed Soliman, Jaime Garrido Aldea, Davy Borowski, Dorye L. Esteras, Neeraj K. Rajak, Niels Chapuis, Abdelkarim Ouerghi, Arnaud Gloppe, Jérôme Robert, Bernard Doudin, Takashi Taniguchi, Kenji Watanabe, José H. García, Stephan Roche, Jean-François Dayen
abstract: Layered A-type antiferromagnetic (AFM) semiconductors offer a unique platform for spintronic devices by combining robust magnetism with gate-tunable semiconducting properties. We present a dual-gate field-effect transistor based on CrSBr, a layered A-type AFM with pronounced transport anisotropy and complex spin dynamics. Our device provides independent control over carrier density and displacement field. Systematic transport measurements reveal that the displacement field, rather than doping, predominantly governs the sign and magnitude of magnetoresistance ratio (MRR). We identify the origins of both negative and positive MRR components and connect them to interlayer and intralayer spin-dependent transport mechanisms. We interpret these findings with ab initio calculations and an effective spin-circuit model that reproduces the anisotropic magnetotransport. Our results identify the displacement field as an efficient electrical control parameter of spin transport in CrSBr and suggest that multi-gate architectures could provide similar control in other layered antiferromagnetic semiconductors.
summary: This work investigates spin transport in layered antiferromagnets using a dual-gate FET structure based on $	ext{CrSBr}$. By combining transport measurements with DFT and spin-circuit modeling, the authors demonstrate that the electric displacement field, not just doping, controls the magnetoresistance. This reveals distinct interlayer and intralayer spin-dependent mechanisms responsible for the observed positive and negative magnetoresistance components.
main_problem: The study aims to microscopically understand the origins of anisotropic magnetoresistance (MRR) and how spin transport in layered antiferromagnets can be electrically controlled.
main_result: The displacement field, rather than carrier doping, is shown to be the dominant electrical control parameter governing the sign and magnitude of the MRR in $	ext{CrSBr}$.
method: The research combines systematic magnetotransport measurements using a dual-gate FET structure with advanced theoretical tools, including DFT calculations and an effective spin-circuit model.
model_or_system: The physical system is a layered A-type antiferromagnetic semiconductor, $	ext{CrSBr}$, fabricated into a dual-gate field-effect transistor. The theoretical framework involves modeling magnetic interactions via a Heisenberg Hamiltonian and calculating magnon-electron scattering effects.
key_observables: Magnetoresistance Ratio (MRR), which exhibits distinct positive (PMR) and negative (NMR) components depending on current and field orientations.
important_parameters: The displacement field ($D$) is highlighted as the crucial control parameter, alongside temperature ($T$) and external magnetic field ($H$).
main_assumptions: The analysis assumes that the observed transport phenomena can be decomposed into contributions from interlayer spin-filtering (negative MRR) and intralayer mechanisms (positive MRR).
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the $	ext{MRR}$ dependence on magnetic field for different current directions ($	ext{I} \parallel a$ vs $	ext{I} \parallel b$), and show band structures confirming weak interlayer coupling.
paper_structure: The paper progresses from experimental characterization of anisotropic magnetotransport in the dual-gate FET to theoretical modeling, identifying the roles of the displacement field, interlayer coupling, and magnon-electron scattering in generating the observed MRR components.
why_interesting: While focused on condensed matter magnetism, the ability to electrically tune spin transport using a displacement field in a layered material provides a model for controlling quantum spin states using external electric fields, relevant to spintronics and quantum information interfaces.

Figure 4 examines the gate dependence of the MRR for a set of gate configurations selected to maximize either D or n, together with several intermediate values. For each trace, we calculated the corresponding D and n. The legend is arranged in ascending order of the MRR value at −3 T. Consistent with the previous observations, the D values follow the trend of the saturated MRR amplitude, whereas the n values show no clear correlation. Remarkably, when I ∥a, this behaviour is observed for all three magnetic-field orientations (a, b, and c).
